title: German grammar
intro: A working reference for beginners to intermediate learners. Every pattern comes with real sentences and a translation: read a section, notice the shape, then listen for it in what you watch and read.

sections.title: Nouns, articles & gender
sections.text: Gender belongs to the word, not to its meaning, so learn every noun together with its article. Endings help: **-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät** are feminine (die Wohnung); **-chen, -lein** are always neuter, even for people (das Mädchen); a person who does something, ending in **-er**, is usually masculine (der Fahrer); most nouns in **-e** are feminine (die Tasche). A compound takes the gender of its last part: das Haus + die Tür → die Haustür. Plurals come in several patterns (Tische, Bücher, Lampen, Autos, Fenster), so learn them with the noun too.

head: Definite
Indefinite
rows: Tische | tables (there is no plural ein)

examples.note: the last part, die Tür, decides the gender

sections.title: Personal pronouns
sections.rule: Pronouns change with their role in the sentence: subject (Nominativ), direct object (Akkusativ) or indirect object (Dativ).
sections.text: A pronoun follows the noun's grammatical gender: der Kaffee → **er**, die Stadt → **sie**, das Buch → **es**. German always says the subject; it never drops it the way Spanish or Japanese do. Use **Sie** (always capitalised) with strangers, at work and in shops; **du** with friends, family, children and online.

examples.text: Der Kaffee ist kalt, er schmeckt nicht.
examples.translation: The coffee is cold; it doesn't taste good.

sections.title: The four cases
sections.text: German shows who does what to whom with **case** endings, mostly on the article. Ask the case question: **Wer?** (Nominativ, the subject), **Wen? Was?** (Akkusativ, the direct object), **Wem?** (Dativ, the indirect object), **Wessen?** (Genitiv, whose).

sections.after: Only the masculine changes in the Akkusativ (der → den, ein → einen). In speech the Genitiv is often replaced by **von + Dativ**: das Auto von meinem Vater.

examples.translation: The dog is looking for the ball.
examples.note: der Hund: subject; den Ball: object
meiner Mutter: Dativ, the person receiving

examples.text: Das Fahrrad meines Bruders ist rot.
examples.note: Genitiv; in speech: das Fahrrad von meinem Bruder

sections.title: Present tense
sections.rule: Take the infinitive, drop -en to get the stem, then add the ending for the person.
sections.text: Stems ending in **-t / -d** add an -e: du arbeit**e**st, er find**e**t. Stems ending in **-s / -ß / -z** take only -t for du: du heißt, du tanzt. Many common irregular verbs change their vowel in the du and er/sie/es forms: **e → i** (sprechen: du sprichst), **e → ie** (lesen: du liest), **a → ä** (fahren: du fährst). The present also covers "I'm doing" and plans: there is no separate continuous form.

examples.translation: She's reading a crime novel at the moment.

sections.title: Essential irregular verbs
sections.text: Learn **sein, haben** and **werden** first: besides their own meaning they build the past (habe gemacht, bin gegangen), the future (werde machen) and the passive.

examples.text: Ich bin müde, aber ich habe Hunger.
Weißt du, wo der Bahnhof ist?
examples.translation: Do you know where the station is?

sections.title: Modal verbs
sections.rule: The modal verb is conjugated in position 2; the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive.
sections.text: The ich and er/sie/es forms are the same and have no ending. Careful: **muss nicht** means "don't have to"; "mustn't" is **darf nicht**. **Will** means "want", not the English future.

examples.translation: You're not allowed to smoke here.
You don't have to do that.

sections.title: Word order: main clauses (verb second)
sections.rule: In a main clause the conjugated verb is always the second element. Whatever comes first (subject, time, place, object), the subject then stands right after the verb.
sections.text: The second part of the verb (infinitive, participle, separable prefix) goes to the very end: Ich **habe** gestern lange **geschlafen**. The connectors **und, aber, oder, denn, sondern** don't take up a position. In the middle of the sentence the usual order is time, reason, manner, place: Ich fahre **morgen** **wegen der Arbeit** **mit dem Zug** **nach Hamburg**.

head: Position 1
Verb
The rest
rows: morgen nach Hamburg. | am going to Hamburg tomorrow.
du morgen nach Hamburg? | Are you going to Hamburg tomorrow?

examples.note: heute takes position 1, so ich follows the verb

examples.text: Am Wochenende habe ich viel geschlafen.
examples.translation: At the weekend I slept a lot.

examples.note: yes/no question: the verb comes first

sections.title: Word order: subordinate clauses (verb last)
sections.rule: After a subordinating conjunction (dass, weil, wenn, als, ob, obwohl, damit, bevor, nachdem …) the conjugated verb moves to the end of its clause. There is always a comma.
sections.text: If the subordinate clause comes first, it counts as position 1, so the main clause starts with its verb: **Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause.** With a modal, the modal is last: …, weil ich arbeiten **muss**. A separable verb joins up again at the end: …, dass er früh **aufsteht**.

examples.text: Ich glaube, dass sie recht hat.
Weil der Zug Verspätung hatte, kam ich zu spät.
examples.translation: Because the train was late, I arrived late.
examples.note: clause first → the main clause starts with the verb

examples.text: Weißt du, ob das Museum heute offen ist?
examples.translation: Do you know whether the museum is open today?

examples.text: Er sagt, dass er früh aufsteht.
examples.translation: He says he gets up early.
examples.note: auf + steht come back together at the end

sections.title: Separable & inseparable verbs
sections.text: Separable prefixes (an, auf, aus, ab, ein, mit, vor, zu, zurück, weg …) are stressed (**AN**rufen) and go to the end of a main clause. Inseparable prefixes (**be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-, miss-**) are unstressed and never move. In the Perfekt, ge- goes between a separable prefix and the stem (an**ge**rufen); inseparable verbs take no ge- (verstanden, bekommen).

Splits?
Verb
In a main clause

Mach bitte die Tür auf. | Please open the door.
Wir kaufen heute ein. | We're going shopping today.
Kommst du mit? | Are you coming along?
Ich verstehe dich. | I understand you.
Sie bekommt ein Paket. | She's getting a parcel.
Er erzählt eine Geschichte. | He's telling a story.

examples.text: Der Film fängt um acht an.

sections.title: Akkusativ vs. Dativ
sections.text: With geben, schenken, zeigen, erklären, schicken, bringen the person is Dativ and the thing Akkusativ. Order: two nouns → Dativ first (Ich gebe **dem Kind** **den Ball**); if the thing is a pronoun, it comes first (Ich gebe **ihn** dem Kind).

head: Akkusativ
Dativ
rows: the direct object: what the action happens to
the indirect object: who receives or benefits
sehen, kaufen, brauchen, haben, finden, suchen
helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, gratulieren, antworten, schmecken, passen

examples.text: Ich zeige dem Gast das Zimmer.
examples.translation: I'm showing the guest the room.
examples.note: dem Gast: Dativ; das Zimmer: Akkusativ

examples.text: Ich danke dir für die Hilfe.

examples.translation: I'll give it to him tomorrow.

sections.title: Two-way prepositions (Wechselpräpositionen)
sections.rule: an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen: movement towards a place → Akkusativ; location → Dativ.
sections.text: The verbs come in pairs: **legen / liegen** (lay / lie), **stellen / stehen** (stand something / stand), **setzen / sitzen** (sit someone / sit), **hängen / hängen**. Short forms: in dem → **im**, in das → **ins**, an dem → **am**, an das → **ans**.

head: Question
Case
Example
rows: Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch. | I put the book on the table.
Das Buch liegt auf dem Tisch. | The book is lying on the table.

examples.text: Häng das Bild an die Wand.
examples.translation: Hang the picture on the wall.

examples.text: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.translation: The picture is hanging on the wall.

sections.title: Perfekt (the spoken past)
sections.rule: haben or sein in position 2 + past participle at the end. In conversation this is the normal past tense.
sections.text: Use **sein** with verbs of movement from A to B (gehen, fahren, fliegen, kommen, laufen), changes of state (aufwachen, einschlafen, sterben, werden) and with sein, bleiben, passieren. Everything else takes **haben**.

head: Verb type
Participle
Example
rows: Ich habe Kaffee gemacht. | I made coffee.
ge- + (changed) stem + -en: schreiben → geschrieben, trinken → getrunken
Sie hat eine E-Mail geschrieben. | She wrote an email.
Wir haben schon eingekauft. | We've already done the shopping.
no ge-: besuchen → besucht, telefonieren → telefoniert
Ich habe Oma besucht. | I visited grandma.

sections.title: Präteritum (the written past)
sections.rule: Stories, news and books use the Präteritum. In speech it's used mainly for sein, haben, the modal verbs and a few others (es gab, ich wusste, ich dachte).
sections.text: Regular verbs add **-te** to the stem. Irregular verbs get a new stem with no ending for ich and er/sie/es: gehen → ging, kommen → kam, sehen → sah, finden → fand, sprechen → sprach.

examples.translation: Once upon a time there was a king.
examples.note: fairy tales and stories use the Präteritum

examples.translation: I had to wait a long time.

sections.title: Futur I
sections.rule: werden in position 2 + infinitive at the end.
sections.text: For plans, German usually just uses the present with a time word: **Morgen fliege ich nach Rom.** Futur I is for promises, predictions and guesses about now (often with **wohl** or **schon**). On its own, **werden** means "to become".

examples.translation: He's going to be a doctor.

sections.title: Reflexive verbs
sections.text: Many verbs are reflexive in German but not in English: **sich freuen** (auf / über), **sich beeilen**, **sich erinnern an**, **sich interessieren für**, **sich setzen**, **sich fühlen**. Use the Dativ form when there is another object: Ich wasche **mir die Hände**.

examples.text: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
examples.translation: I'm looking forward to the weekend.

examples.note: mir: die Zähne is the direct object

sections.title: Adjective endings
sections.rule: An adjective before a noun takes an ending. If the article already shows gender and case (der, dem), the adjective just takes -e or -en. If it doesn't (ein, or no article at all), the adjective shows it (-er, -es).

tables.caption: After der, die, das (and dieser, jeder, welcher)
head: Masc.
Fem.
Neuter
Plural

sections.after: After the noun, with sein or werden, there is no ending: Das Hemd ist **neu**.

examples.translation: I'm looking for a cheap flat.

examples.text: Mit dem neuen Handy bin ich zufrieden.
examples.translation: I'm happy with the new phone.

sections.title: Comparatives & superlatives
sections.text: "Than" is **als**: größer als ich. "As … as" is **so … wie**: so groß wie du. Short adjectives often take an umlaut (alt → älter). Before a noun the forms take normal adjective endings: das schneller**e** Auto, der höchst**e** Berg.

examples.text: Mein Bruder ist so alt wie du.
examples.translation: My brother is as old as you.
Pasta is what I like eating most.

examples.text: Die Zugspitze ist der höchste Berg Deutschlands.
examples.translation: The Zugspitze is Germany's highest mountain.

sections.title: Question words (W-Fragen)
sections.text: The question word takes position 1 and the verb follows. With a preposition, things become **wo(r)- + preposition**: Worauf wartest du? (What are you waiting for?) Wofür ist das? (What's that for?) For people you keep the preposition: Auf wen wartest du?

Meaning
Example

Wer kommt mit? | Who's coming along?
Wen hast du gesehen? | Who did you see?
Wem gehört das? | Who does this belong to?
Wo ist die Toilette? | Where's the toilet?
Wohin fährst du? | Where are you going?
Woher kommst du? | Where are you from?
Wann beginnt der Kurs? | When does the course start?

Wie heißt du? | What's your name?
Welche Farbe magst du? | Which colour do you like?
Wie viele Leute kommen? | How many people are coming?

sections.title: Negation: nicht vs. kein
sections.text: **Nicht** goes to the end of the clause, or right before what it negates (an adjective, a place, a phrase with a preposition): Ich wohne **nicht in Berlin**. After a negation, "but" is **sondern**. Useful: **noch nicht** (not yet), **nicht mehr** (no longer), **kein … mehr** (no more), **nie** (never), **nichts** (nothing), **niemand** (nobody).

head: Use
When
Example
rows: a noun that would have ein, or no article
Ich habe kein Auto. | I don't have a car.
everything else: verbs, adjectives, nouns with der/die/das, names
Das ist nicht mein Auto. | That isn't my car.

examples.text: Das ist nicht teuer, sondern billig.

sections.title: Relative clauses
sections.rule: The relative pronoun takes its gender and number from the noun it refers to, and its case from its role in the relative clause. The verb goes to the end, with commas around the clause.

examples.text: Der Mann, der dort steht, ist mein Nachbar.
examples.translation: The man who's standing there is my neighbour.

examples.text: Das ist die Frau, die ich gestern getroffen habe.
examples.translation: That's the woman I met yesterday.

examples.text: Die Freunde, mit denen ich reise, kommen aus Köln.
examples.translation: The friends I'm travelling with are from Cologne.

sections.title: Konjunktiv II (would, could, if only)
sections.text: Use it for things that aren't real (Wenn ich Zeit **hätte**, **würde** ich mehr lesen), for polite requests (**Könnten** Sie …? Ich **hätte** gern …) and advice (An deiner Stelle **würde** ich …). For most verbs use würde + infinitive; sein, haben and the modals have their own forms. For the past: hätte / wäre + participle.

examples.text: Wenn ich reich wäre, würde ich reisen.
examples.translation: If I were rich, I would travel.

sections.title: Commands (imperative)
sections.text: The du form drops -st and the pronoun (du kommst → **Komm!**). Verbs with e → i keep the i (nimm, lies, gib, sprich), but a → ä does not carry over (fahr!). **Bitte, doch, mal** make it friendlier: Komm doch mal vorbei! "Let's …" is **Gehen wir!** or **Lass uns gehen!**

sections.title: Prepositions & their cases
sections.text: Common short forms: zu dem → **zum**, zu der → **zur**, bei dem → **beim**, von dem → **vom**. In speech, wegen and trotz often take the Dativ: wegen dem Regen.

head: Case
Prepositions
Example
rows: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um, bis, entlang
Das Geschenk ist für dich. | The present is for you.
aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu, gegenüber, ab

an, auf, hinter, in, neben, über, unter, vor, zwischen
Akkusativ for direction, Dativ for location (see two-way prepositions)
Wegen des Regens bleiben wir drinnen. | Because of the rain we're staying in.

examples.translation: After the meal we're going for a walk.

head: Don't confuse
Difference
Example
rows: know a fact vs. be familiar with a person, place or thing
Ich weiß, wo er wohnt. | I know where he lives. ;; Ich kenne ihn gut. | I know him well.
als: one event in the past; wenn: whenever, if, or in the future; wann: the question 'when?'
Als ich Kind war … | When I was a child … ;; Wenn ich Zeit habe … | When(ever) I have time …
for or since (still going: present tense) vs. ago
Ich wohne seit 2020 hier. | I've lived here since 2020. ;; vor zwei Jahren | two years ago
Ich bekomme ein Geschenk. | I'm getting a present. ;; Ich werde müde. | I'm getting tired.
gern + verb: like doing; mögen + noun: like a thing; gefallen + Dativ: appeal to
Ich koche gern. | I like cooking. ;; Das Lied gefällt mir. | I like the song.
nach: towns, countries, home; zu: people, places, buildings
nach Berlin | to Berlin ;; zum Arzt | to the doctor's
Ich bin zu Hause. | I'm at home. ;; Ich gehe nach Hause. | I'm going home.
sondern corrects a negation; aber adds a contrast
nicht heute, sondern morgen | not today but tomorrow ;; teuer, aber gut | expensive but good
Ich lerne Deutsch. | I'm learning German. ;; Sie studiert Medizin. | She's studying medicine.
you (formal) vs. she vs. they: the verb and the capital letter tell
Sie kommt. | She's coming. ;; Kommen Sie? | Are you coming?

sections.title: One-page memory map
points: Learn der, die or das with every noun; meaning doesn't tell you the gender.
The four cases show who does what to whom, so the word order can move around.
The conjugated verb is second in a main clause and last in a subordinate clause.
Separable prefixes go to the end; be-, ver-, er- and friends never move.
Perfekt: sein for movement and change, haben for almost everything else.
helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören and a few more always take the Dativ.
Two-way prepositions: direction (wohin?) → Akkusativ, location (wo?) → Dativ.
kein negates nouns with ein or no article; nicht negates everything else.
würde + infinitive covers most "would"; wäre, hätte and könnte have their own forms.
Adjective endings depend on what comes before them: a der-word, an ein-word or nothing.
sections.tip: Reading strategy: find the conjugated verb first (it tells you who is doing what), then look at the end of the clause for the piece that completes it: a separable prefix, a participle or an infinitive.
